claims.text: Enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower effective melting temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio lowers the free-energy barrier for nanoparticle melting.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic and as-synthesized.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles typically have FCC or multiply twinned structures.
Replica-exchange MD or metadynamics can compute temperature-dependent free-energy profiles for these nanoparticles.
Accurately parameterized interatomic potentials are needed for the proposed simulations.
A controlled temperature ramp can cover solid, premelted, and melted nanoparticle states.
Nanoparticles with diameters of approximately 3 nm, 5 nm, and 10 nm can be compared to determine size dependence.
Decreasing nanoparticle size increases the relative contribution of surface atoms compared with core atoms.
The surface-to-core contribution mediates the onset and progression of atomic disorder and melting.
The increased proportion of surface atoms in smaller nanoparticles lowers the free-energy barrier for atomic rearrangement during heating.
The lower rearrangement barrier causes smaller nanoparticles to begin melting at lower temperatures.
Decreasing nanoparticle size will produce measurable decreases in melting temperature or free-energy barrier and therefore reduced thermal stability.
Standard MD without enhanced sampling may fail to capture the full free-energy landscape of phase transitions in multicomponent systems.
The predicted observations depend on the accuracy of the interatomic potential.
Quantum-size effects and nonspherical morphology may alter the thermal response of very small nanoparticles.
The magnitude of melting-temperature reduction may depend on morphology, potential accuracy, and simulation parameters.
Free-energy calculations and coexistence simulations can be used to predict melting points.
The hypothesis is falsified if size-dependent differences in melting temperature or free-energy barrier do not exceed simulation error margins.
